windows.text: Mitochondrial and cellular energy starvation is what you get when there's not enough of the fuels each type of cell in your gut prefers (glutamine and butyrate). Your gut barrier needs a lot of energy, to keep its tight junctions intact. If the cells lining your small intestine (called enterocytes) or the colonocytes lining your large intestine don't do that, the barrier loosens up. Then lipopolysaccharides (LPS, which come from the walls of bacteria) and other endotoxins leak through those (not-so-tight)-junction gaps into your bloodstream.

windows.label: Human Written
windows.text: L-Glutamine (watch Dr. Rhonda vid) is the main fuel for your enterocytes, and for your immune cells when they're activated. It doesn't have to go through the complicated digestive steps other nutrients do.

windows.label: Human Written
windows.text: Inside the mitochondria, it gets turned straight into alpha-ketoglutarate, or α-KG. The α-KG goes into the citric acid cycle, which is how the mitochondria make their energy.

windows.label: Human Written
windows.text: So that's why consuming pure glutamine gives energy to those cells faster than eating food. They then use their extra energy to repair the gut lining by pulling the tight junctions together, and that keeps LPS from getting through.

windows.label: Human Written
windows.text: Glutamine also provides nitrogen to help build new cells.

windows.text: Malic and citric acid (which make green apples and tart cherries sour) are made and used partway round that same cycle, also called the TCA or Krebs cycle, so in theory they're a quick energy source for your enterocytes too.

windows.label: AI-Generated
windows.text: But there's no good evidence they add much fuel on top of what glutamine gives.

windows.label: AI-Generated
windows.text: The better reason to eat them is iron: they help keep the iron in a meal dissolved, so more of it gets absorbed.

windows.label: AI-Assisted
windows.text: In one study, adding 1 g of pure malic or citric acid to a rice meal raised how much of its iron people absorbed two to three times, and the vegetables whose iron was well absorbed had a good amount of these acids in them (Gillooly et al., 1983).
